transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-09-17 15:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Samira Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Riley Tan (Redwood PE - sat in), Alex Mercer (NovusRx CTO), Priya Shah (NovusRx SRE), Maya Lin (Product Manager), Ethan Park (Backend), Liam Ortiz (Security)

Summary:
Quick console walkthrough focused on tracing, request logs, and error triage. Customer wants clearer visibility into token-level latency, failure root cause, and how to run replays against suspect requests. Discussed hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, VPC options, and security controls. Agreed next steps: send SOC2/security deck, create trial tenant, share redacted logs for replay.

Topics covered:
- Navigation of Console trace timeline and request-level breadcrumbs
- Request playback/replay and replay artifacts (KV cache mismatch scenarios)
- Error classification and automated anomaly detection (regression alerts)
- RBAC, KMS, audit logs and VPC/private deployment notes
- Batching/caching tradeoffs and how they show up in request traces

Transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Okay cool good morning everyone or afternoon I guess, thanks for joining. This is Samira from Redwood, I'll run the intro and then Diego will demo the console.
[00:18] Alex: Hey thanks, appreciate it. We're mostly interested in how we can quickly surface root cause for these model failures that are leaking into production.
[00:32] Diego: Right totally. The plan for today is show tracing, request logs, a replay, and then a short look at the security controls. We'll try to hit one failing trace from Priya's examples.
[00:45] Priya: Yep I dropped three logs into the folder you gave earlier, they are redacted. One is a KV cache mismatch thing, another looks like long tail latency, and one is a 500 from a third-party preprocessor.
[00:58] Diego: Great, we'll pull those in. Quick note: sometimes our transcript tool writes KV cache as K-V cash in the UI, so apologies if you see that in the export, it's the same thing.
[01:12] Riley: and just to add, for context, NovusRx mentioned the requests are mostly short medical summarization prompts, 200-400 token outputs, bursts durante batch jobs overnight.
[01:29] Maya: Right and our SLO is 95th percentile under 220ms at 400 tokens, anything beyond that we treat as an incident.
[01:39] Diego: Cool. Okay I'm sharing my screen, Console > Requests > Trace inspector. You'll see the timeline across the top with request spans, these are autolinked to the model variant and the batch size used.
[01:55] [02:05] Diego: Here, this trace was captured at 02:14 UTC — you can see the green/amber/red bands: green is prefix caching hit, amber indicates KV cache warm (that means partial cache), red is cold path where we did a full model forward.
[02:25] Ethan: Wait what is the amber exactly, is that an approximate cache or like partial tokens?
[02:32] Diego: Good question—amber indicates prefix matched but KV entries were partial so the runtime did some cache fill. That can cause small spikes. You'll see the token timing waterfall on the right.
[02:48] Alex: How do we correlate this to our logs? We ingest through CloudWatch and Splunk.
[02:56] Diego: Two ways. One is the request-id header mapped in the trace, you can use the trace id to search in Splunk. The other is the export link — we can push a JSON artifact with the request timeline.
[03:12] Priya: And does the Console show the prompt and the model responses? We can't share full PII, so we need redaction controls.
[03:20] Samira: Yes we have redaction and data retention controls. For Private customers you can configure no retention or token-level stripping at ingestion. We'll share the security doc.
[03:34] [03:45] Diego: Back to the trace — I'm going to cherry-pick the failing trace Priya uploaded. Here you can see a spike at token 34, there's a sudden 450ms per-token jump. If I expand the event, it shows an external pre-processing call timing out and returning an error code which triggered fallback logic.
[04:02] Priya: That matches our notes, the preprocessor times out under load and then their client retries which multiplies.
[04:12] Diego: Exactly. Console has a request replay capability — we'll run the replay against a sandbox model variant. When we replay, the runtime will show KV cache seed state, and whether we're hitting cold paths.
[04:28] Alex: When you replay, will it consume tokens or cost us? We want to avoid incurring too much during debugging.
[04:34] Diego: Replays do not bill at the hosted production rate; for the trial we can enable replay-cost-free mode, or run it on a dedicated sandbox. We can also sample tokens or run a dry-run which logs timings without materializing tokens.
[04:51] Liam: For security, how is the replay data stored? Is that in the same audit trail as normal requests?
[04:58] Samira: Yes it's captured in the audit logs and marked trace:replay. For private deployments, the artifacts stay inside your VPC storage and can be routed to your S3 with SSE-KMS.
[05:14] [05:30] Diego: Kicking off the replay now — you'll see a new request event appear in the timeline. We also show the difference heatmap vs the original capture; red cells are slower tokens, green are faster.
[05:45] Priya: I'm seeing a divergent path in the replay, looks like the KV cache seed was empty in replay environment.
[05:52] Diego: Mhmm, that's common. In production, KV cache was warm thanks to prior user interactions. When you replay from a cold environment you may trigger cold-path skew. We surface a "cache mismatch" note and provide an option to seed the KV state from a snapshot.
[06:12] Riley: We're going to demo that — selecting seed state -> choose snapshot -> replay with seeded state.
[06:22] [06:40] Diego: Replay completed; the latency curve now matches original and the token spike disappears. That indicates the preprocessor still had a transient problem, but the big contributor was the cold path.
[06:53] Alex: Good, so that gives us guidance to address both client-side timeouts and ensure warm-up before bursts.
[07:02] Maya: One thing—how do we set up alerts when token latency regresses for specific prompts? We want to catch model drift or perf regressions.
[07:12] Diego: You can create promptset-based quality monitors in Optimize — tie prompts to evals and set regression thresholds. In the Console you can create an alert rule for token-timing anomalies for specific routes or model tags.
[07:28] Samira: We'll share a short doc about Optimize's promptset monitoring and how it maps to Console alerts.
[07:36] [07:52] Ethan: On the networking front: we have a strict egress policy, so any outbound call from the runtime must go through our NAT. If we run Redwood Private on-prem, how do third-party preprocessors work?
[08:02] Diego: In Private you can configure the runtime to call internal endpoints only, or route through your egress with proxies. If a third-party is required, you can establish a VPC endpoint or use a dedicated egress cluster. We'll put details in the architecture slide.
[08:18] Liam: And one more — KMS integration for key wrapping; do we have HSM support?
[08:24] Samira: We do KMS and HSM via customer-managed key material in our Private distribution. For hosted we offer envelope encryption using customer KMS via interconnects.
[08:36] [08:50] Diego: Switching to error analysis — here's the Error Summary view. We cluster errors by fingerprint: stack, error code, and failing span. You can click into a cluster and see sample requests, the top contributing prompts, and a small diff of token latency.
[09:06] Priya: How noisy is that clustering? We have a lot of transient timeouts, want to avoid alert fatigue.
[09:13] Diego: You can tune thresholds and merge clusters, or mark certain endpoints as noisy with suppression windows. We also support labels so SREs can triage and mute while investigating.
[09:28] Alex: Any pre-built integrations for our pager/ops toolchain? We run PagerDuty and DataDog.
[09:34] Samira: Yes we have webhooks and native integrations for PD and Datadog. The alerts include trace links and replay buttons.
[09:44] [10:05] Diego: I want to show an example of a regression alert: here's a route that saw a 30% increase in 95th percentile. Click "Investigate" — Console surfaces the promptset, recent deploys, model variants and any config changes. You can roll back to a pinned model version directly from this UI.
[10:28] Maya: Is rollback instantaneous? Won't that cause inconsistency given ongoing requests?
[10:34] Diego: We do an atomic route update which directs new requests to the fallback variant; existing in-flight requests finish on the previous variant. For canary rollouts you can set traffic percentages and automatic fallback if QoS degrades.
[10:50] [11:10] Alex: Going back to the KV cache talk — can we debug cache corruption? We saw one observed output mismatch that looked like tokens from a different user.
[11:20] Diego: That's rare; our traces include KV key hashes and provenance. If you suspect cross-tenant contamination in a Dedicated or Private set-up, we can collect a binary KV snapshot and run assertion checks. We'll need to run that in a controlled environment.
[11:38] Priya: We'll need SLAs on that investigation and access controls.
[11:44] Samira: Agreed — we'll put an escalation path into the support runbook we share.
[11:54] [12:05] Diego: Now quick perf note: batching increases throughput but can add queue wait time for low QPS routes. Console shows queue wait and batch size distribution per route so you can tune batching windows.
[12:20] Ethan: We saw spikes at 03:00 local due to batch jobs — how do we carve out capacity?
[12:27] Diego: You can reserve a Dedicated pool for heavy batch jobs or use priority routing to route batch jobs to cheaper slower variants while keeping fast variants for interactive requests.
[12:40] [12:58] Alex: On pricing — is Dedicated monthly or annual, and does it include the Console?
[13:05] Samira: Dedicated is commit-based (monthly or annual), Console is included. There are add-ons for extended telemetry retention and enterprise SLAs. We'll send a pricing summary.
[13:20] [13:45] Diego: Time to demo the request log search. Type a fuzzy string or paste the request id; we have fuzzy matching and a quick filter on error code, model tag, and route.
[13:58] Priya: I'm searching using our request id — here, found it, but transcript shows some garbling in the prompt.
[14:06] Diego: That's likely the transcript generator, but the raw request payload is downloadable.
[14:14] Maya: Is the raw payload stored encrypted?
[14:18] Samira: Yes encrypted at rest with customer-managed keys in Private; hosted also encrypted and we support short TTLs.
[14:30] [14:45] Diego: Now let's run a small live load of 200 parallel requests in the sandbox so you can watch traces come in real time. We'll limit to the test tenant so no billing incidents.
[15:00] Alex: Go for it.
[15:20] [15:50] Diego: You can see a spike of amber traces—partial cache warmups. After a warm up period, the distribution settles. Console provides a "warm up" script you can run before heavy batch loads.
[16:10] Priya: That script — is it idempotent? We want to schedule a warm-up job that doesn't affect user-facing logs.
[16:17] Diego: It's idempotent; it uses synthetic prompts and can be configured to go to a shadow model variant to avoid impacting metrics.
[16:32] Maya: On the topic of privacy, we need audit trails per token access. Is that available?
[16:39] Samira: We capture token-level events for private deployments and can export a token audit for compliance reviews; we avoid storing PII in plain text for hosted customers unless explicit retention is enabled.
[16:54] [17:10] Diego: Let's pivot to a debugging flow: triage -> reproduce -> replay -> fix -> verify. I'll mark the steps in the Console: tag, add note, assign to SRE, kick replay.
[17:26] Ethan: Can we attach runbooks into an action so it's part of the ticket?
[17:30] Diego: Yep you can attach runbook snippets and link to a Confluence page. The action becomes part of the trace ticket.
[17:40] Alex: For the POC, what do you need from us?
[17:44] Samira: Redacted failing logs, success criteria doc, and a contact for engineering access. Diego will set up the trial tenant.
[17:56] [18:12] Priya: One more nit — when we export traces to Splunk, can we get the same token timings or just high-level spans?
[18:20] Diego: We export full JSON timelines with per-token timing if you want it; Splunk ingest might need a custom parser but we can provide a transform.
[18:32] Liam: Security question — who can access replay artifacts in the Console? We need RBAC on replay and ability to mask fields per role.
[18:40] Samira: You can create roles: TraceViewer (read-only), TraceEngineer (can run replays), TraceAdmin (manage snapshots). We also support field-level redaction via policy.
[18:54] [19:10] Alex: Okay that covers most of our concerns. Could you show a short example of a failed 500 from a third-party?
[19:17] Diego: Sure — here's that trace. The preprocessor returned 502, you can expand the HTTP span and see headers and latency. The stack trace shows the retry loop. We recommend adding a short circuit/retry policy to avoid amplification.
[19:34] Maya: Can we set auto-suppress for a transient 502?
[19:38] Diego: Yes we have suppression windows and learned suppression for flappers.
[19:45] [20:05] Samira: Quick recap then we'll close: deliverables — SOC2/security deck (Samira), trial tenant and replay run (Diego), redacted logs (Priya), define SLOs doc (Maya). We'll follow up to schedule a POC kick-off.
[20:28] Alex: Looks good, thanks everyone.
[20:32] Priya: Thanks, that was useful.
[20:40] Diego: Thanks all. Ending recording.
